You are coding NSW motor accident decisions for a research dataset. Read the decision text supplied and assign each ordinal score from the text alone.

Score each dimension INDEPENDENTLY. A decision describing a severe case will score high on some dimensions and not others: severe physical injury does not by itself imply a contested proceeding, a disputed liability, or a prominent psychological component. Judge each scale against its own definition and resist letting an overall impression of severity carry across the scales.

If the text does not support a judgement on a dimension, give the lowest score rather than guessing upward, and say so in `uncertain`.

DECISION TEXT:
--- Catchwords ---
MOTOR ACCIDENTS -

Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017 ; damages assessment; liability admitted; claimant beauty therapist sustained multiple orthopaedic injuries in high-impact collision; combined impairment below 10% precluding non-economic loss; dispute as to extent of economic loss; claimant returned to modified work with reduced hours and capacity; evidence supported ongoing but not total incapacity; no sufficient basis for early retirement or loss of chance to establish own business; future loss assessed on reduced weekly earning capacity with conventional vicissitudes; statutory benefits not treated as earnings but insurer entitled to credit; Fox v Wood component considered. Held – damages assessed at $316,534.95 including past and future economic loss, and superannuation.

--- Key Paragraphs ---
[para 2] Records combined WPI at 6% and confirms non‑economic loss not available; frames damages heads.
2. The amount of the claimant's costs in the matter is $41,165.26 inclusive of GST. A statement setting out the Commission's reasons for the assessment is included with this certificate.

STATEMENT OF REASONS

INTRODUCTION

[para 22] Rejects optimistic full‑time return; prefers guarded evidence; central to capacity findings.
22. I do not accept that the claimant's disabilities are confined to some modest or temporary reduction capable of resolution in the near future. Dr Hyde-Page was optimistic that, with strengthening and possibly further treatment, the claimant should be able to return to full-time work over 12 to 24 months. I do not reject that opinion lightly. However, it is now almost four years since the accident. The claimant's hours had reduced to 24 to 25 per week by mid-November 2025. The employer's material does not suggest a trajectory of return to full-time work; rather, it describes the ongoing need to customise duties and hours to the claimant's reduced capabilities. The functional evidence of Ms Moretti, and the practical vocational evidence of Mr Manca, are also inconsistent with any present confidence that a return to full-time pre-injury work is likely within a short timeframe. In that respect I prefer the more guarded views of Dr Bodel and Ms Moretti.

[para 23] Rejects early retirement finding due to insufficient evidentiary basis.
23. That said, I am not satisfied that the evidence establishes, in any reliable way, that the claimant will retire 10 years early or that there is a presently proven trajectory of progressive deterioration sufficient to justify such a finding. Dr Bodel did express the opinion that, as the claimant ages, her symptoms will deteriorate and that it is unlikely she will remain in full-time beauty therapy work until retirement age. But the opinion, in my view, remained general in nature. It was not tied to a specific timeframe or to a clearly reasoned pathway from these injuries to retirement at age 60. The claimant properly accepted in oral submissions that there was no specific medical basis for the ten-year figure. Further, the orthopaedic evidence was not all one way, and Dr Hyde-Page expressly anticipated further improvement rather than deterioration. I therefore find that the claimant's present work restrictions are ongoing and significant, and likely durable, but I am not satisfied that the evidence permits a finding that the accident will probably shorten her working life by 10 years. Past economic loss

[para 24] Allows past economic loss; anchors quantum foundation.
24. I accept the claimant's past economic loss claim in the sum of $105,241.

[para 28] Clarifies statutory benefits are not earnings for assessing past loss; legal treatment.
28. Nor do I consider it appropriate, in these reasons, to treat the insurer's payments as generating some free-standing "credit" which extinguishes the claimant's common law claim for past economic loss. The question whether statutory benefits already paid are to be repaid, refunded or otherwise brought to account is governed by the Motor Accident Injuries Act 2017 (NSW) and the mechanisms it provides. That is distinct from the present task of assessing the damages to which the claimant is otherwise entitled. The associated tax component is separately addressed by the claimant's Fox v Wood claim.

[para 36] Declines separate open‑labour‑market buffer; avoids double counting.
36. Nor am I persuaded that a separate substantial buffer should be allowed on the footing that the claimant is likely to be thrown onto the open labour market and thereby sustain some much greater future loss. I accept that her present employer is supportive and accommodating. I also accept that, if the claimant were required to seek alternative work, she may encounter real difficulty obtaining employment of the same kind and under equally accommodating conditions. But there are several reasons why I do not consider it appropriate to translate that risk into a distinct large monetary allowance. First, the claimant remains employed, is valued by her employer, and retains a clientele. Second, no evidence was adduced from the employer suggesting that the current arrangements are precarious or likely to end. The evidence rises no higher than the claimant's speculation that her employer may not continue to accommodate her restrictions into the future. Third, the very matters said to justify a labour market buffer are already reflected, at least substantially, in the acceptance that the claimant's ongoing earning capacity is now materially reduced. To allow a large further sum on that basis would risk double counting.

[para 38] Adopts average net weekly differential of 225; sets method for future loss.
38. In assessing future economic loss, I treat the claimant's oral evidence at the assessment conference as significant. In cross-examination, she accepted that the present difference between her pre-accident earnings and her current earnings was about $200 net per week, whilst acknowledging some fluctuation. I regard that concession as the proper present starting point. I do not, however, consider it appropriate to assume that the differential would remain fixed in nominal terms over the balance of her working life. Had the accident not occurred, it is more probable than not that her earnings would have increased over time, at least modestly, by reason of ordinary wage movement and CPI-type indexation. Adopting a broad evaluative approach, rather than undertaking a year-by-year indexed calculation, I assess the claimant's future loss on the basis of an average net weekly differential of $225, reflecting a modest uplift on the presently accepted differential to allow for ordinary wage movement and CPI-type indexation over time.

[para 40] Performs multiplier and vicissitudes; quantifies future economic loss at 169,218.
40.

I also do not consider that the claimant should be assessed on the footing of working to age 70. Having regard to the physical nature of beauty therapy work, which requires prolonged standing, repeated use of the upper limbs, dexterity and stamina, I consider that a retirement age of 65 is the more realistic assumption. The claimant was 29 years of age at the time of assessment. Applying the 5% multiplier for 36 years, namely 884.8, to a weekly loss of $225, and allowing the conventional deduction of 15% for vicissitudes, I assess future economic loss at $169,218. I allow that sum. Future loss of superannuation
